questions.question: Why does Brutus decide that Caesar must die before becoming king?

options.text: He fears that royal power may turn Caesar into a tyrant.
He knows Caesar has already condemned him to death.
He wants Antony to inherit Caesar’s authority.
He has discovered that Caesar forged citizens’ letters.

questions.explanation: Brutus admits no personal grievance and reasons from the danger Caesar might become if crowned.

evidence.exact:
BRUTUS.
It must be by his death: and for my part,
I know no personal cause to spurn at him,
But for the general. He would be crown’d:
How that might change his nature, there’s the question.
It is the bright day that brings forth the adder,
And that craves wary walking. Crown him?—that;
And then, I grant, we put a sting in him,
That at his will he may do danger with.
Th’ abuse of greatness is, when it disjoins
Remorse from power; and, to speak truth of Caesar,
I have not known when his affections sway’d
More than his reason. But ’tis a common proof,
That lowliness is young ambition’s ladder,
Whereto the climber-upward turns his face;
But when he once attains the upmost round,
He then unto the ladder turns his back,
Looks in the clouds, scorning the base degrees
By which he did ascend. So Caesar may;
Then lest he may, prevent. And since the quarrel
Will bear no colour for the thing he is,
Fashion it thus: that what he is, augmented,
Would run to these and these extremities:
And therefore think him as a serpent’s egg
Which hatch’d, would, as his kind grow mischievous;
And kill him in the shell.

questions.question: How does Cassius plan to influence Brutus with letters?

options.text: Read Caesar’s genuine will to Brutus in public.
Make forged writings appear to come from several citizens.
Send Brutus a confession signed by Antony.
Intercept orders from Octavius to the Senate.

questions.explanation: Cassius plans letters in different hands praising Brutus and hinting at Caesar’s ambition.

evidence.exact:
Well, Brutus, thou art noble; yet I see,
Thy honourable metal may be wrought
From that it is dispos’d: therefore ’tis meet
That noble minds keep ever with their likes;
For who so firm that cannot be seduc’d?
Caesar doth bear me hard, but he loves Brutus.
If I were Brutus now, and he were Cassius,
He should not humour me. I will this night,
In several hands, in at his windows throw,
As if they came from several citizens,
Writings, all tending to the great opinion
That Rome holds of his name; wherein obscurely
Caesar’s ambition shall be glanced at.
And after this, let Caesar seat him sure,
For we will shake him, or worse days endure.

questions.question: Why does Brutus oppose killing Antony along with Caesar?

options.text: He has promised to make Antony king after Caesar.
He believes Antony has already agreed to join them.
He thinks further killing would make their cause seem bloody and envious.
He wants Antony to command their army at Philippi.

questions.explanation: Brutus wants their act to look like a necessary sacrifice rather than butchery, and dismisses Antony as Caesar’s dependent.

evidence.exact:
BRUTUS.
Our course will seem too bloody, Caius Cassius,
To cut the head off, and then hack the limbs,
Like wrath in death, and envy afterwards;
For Antony is but a limb of Caesar.
Let us be sacrificers, but not butchers, Caius.
We all stand up against the spirit of Caesar,
And in the spirit of men there is no blood.
O, that we then could come by Caesar’s spirit,
And not dismember Caesar! But, alas,
Caesar must bleed for it! And, gentle friends,
Let’s kill him boldly, but not wrathfully;
Let’s carve him as a dish fit for the gods,
Not hew him as a carcass fit for hounds.
And let our hearts, as subtle masters do,
Stir up their servants to an act of rage,
And after seem to chide ’em. This shall mark
Our purpose necessary, and not envious;
Which so appearing to the common eyes,
We shall be call’d purgers, not murderers.
And for Mark Antony, think not of him;
For he can do no more than Caesar’s arm
When Caesar’s head is off.

questions.question: How does Decius counter Calphurnia’s warning dream?

options.text: He says the dream names Brutus as Caesar’s successor.
He claims the dream orders Caesar to flee to Sardis.
He interprets the blood as Antony’s death at Philippi.
He interprets the blood as life and honor flowing from Caesar to Rome.

questions.explanation: Decius turns the frightening image into a flattering promise that Rome will draw reviving blood from Caesar.

evidence.exact:
DECIUS.
This dream is all amiss interpreted:
It was a vision fair and fortunate.
Your statue spouting blood in many pipes,
In which so many smiling Romans bath’d,
Signifies that from you great Rome shall suck
Reviving blood, and that great men shall press
For tinctures, stains, relics, and cognizance.
This by Calphurnia’s dream is signified.

evidence.suffix:
CAESAR.
And this way have you

questions.question: What restriction does Brutus place on Antony’s funeral speech?

options.text: Antony may praise Caesar but must not blame the conspirators.
Antony must defend the assassination before praising Caesar.
Antony may speak only if Cassius reads Caesar’s will.
Antony must leave Rome before addressing the citizens.

questions.explanation: Brutus allows praise of Caesar while forbidding Antony to blame those who killed him.

evidence.exact:
BRUTUS.
Mark Antony, here, take you Caesar’s body.
You shall not in your funeral speech blame us,
But speak all good you can devise of Caesar,
And say you do’t by our permission;
Else shall you not have any hand at all
About his funeral. And you shall speak
In the same pulpit whereto I am going,
After my speech is ended.
evidence.prefix: what may fall; I like it not.

questions.question: What does Antony reveal from Caesar’s will to strengthen the crowd’s attachment to Caesar?

options.text: An order appointing Cassius ruler of Rome.
A gift of money to every Roman citizen.
A pardon for the men who would kill Caesar.
A command that Brutus marry Calphurnia.

questions.explanation: The announced gift of seventy-five drachmas to each citizen prompts cries for revenge.

evidence.exact:
ANTONY.
Here is the will, and under Caesar’s seal.
To every Roman citizen he gives,
To every several man, seventy-five drachmas.
evidence.prefix: let’s stay, and hear the will.

questions.question: Why does the mob attack Cinna the poet despite his denial of involvement in the conspiracy?

options.text: He admits that he struck Caesar in the Senate.
He refuses to surrender Caesar’s will to Antony.
His name matches that of a conspirator, and the mob disregards the distinction.
He tries to recruit the crowd for Cassius’s army.

questions.explanation: The citizens continue threatening him even after he identifies himself as the poet rather than the conspirator.

evidence.exact:
CINNA.
I am Cinna the poet, I am Cinna the poet.
evidence.suffix:
FOURTH CITIZEN.
Tear him for h

evidence.exact:
FOURTH CITIZEN.
It is no matter, his name’s Cinna; pluck but his name out of his heart, and turn him going.

questions.question: Why does Brutus favor marching to Philippi rather than waiting for the enemy?

options.text: He believes his army needs to retreat to recover its strength.
He wants the enemy to exhaust itself reaching his camp.
He hopes to avoid a battle until Caesar’s funeral.
He wants to prevent the enemy gaining recruits on its advance.

questions.explanation: Brutus argues that meeting the enemy at Philippi denies it support from the intervening population.

evidence.exact:
BRUTUS.
Good reasons must of force give place to better.
The people ’twixt Philippi and this ground
Do stand but in a forced affection;
For they have grudg’d us contribution.
The enemy, marching along by them,
By them shall make a fuller number up,
Come on refresh’d, new-added, and encourag’d;
From which advantage shall we cut him off
If at Philippi we do face him there,
These people at our back.

questions.question: What mistaken report helps drive Cassius to have himself killed?

options.text: That Titinius has been captured by enemy horsemen.
That Brutus has accepted a crown from Octavius.
That Antony has died while addressing the citizens.
That Caesar has returned alive to command the army.

questions.explanation: Pindarus reports Titinius surrounded and taken; Cassius believes his friend lost.

evidence.exact:
PINDARUS.
[Above.] Titinius is enclosed round about
With horsemen, that make to him on the spur,
Yet he spurs on. Now they are almost on him.
Now, Titinius! Now some light. O, he lights too.
He’s ta’en!

CASSIUS.
Come down; behold no more.
O, coward that I am, to live so long,
To see my best friend ta’en before my face!
evidence.prefix: And, hark! they shout for joy.

questions.question: How does Antony distinguish Brutus from the other conspirators after Brutus’s death?

options.text: He says Brutus never took part in Caesar’s killing.
He says Brutus acted for the common good rather than envy.
He says Brutus fought secretly on Octavius’s side.
He says Brutus valued wealth above Rome’s welfare.

questions.explanation: Antony credits Brutus alone among the conspirators with an honest concern for the public good.

evidence.exact:
ANTONY.
This was the noblest Roman of them all.
All the conspirators save only he,
Did that they did in envy of great Caesar;
He only, in a general honest thought
And common good to all, made one of them.
His life was gentle, and the elements
So mix’d in him that Nature might stand up
And say to all the world, “This was a man!”
